questions.stem: A spinner is spun 80 times. It lands on red 22 times. What is the relative frequency of landing on red?
questions.explanation: Relative frequency = number of successes / total trials = 22/80 = 0.275. Option (b) divides by the number of non-red outcomes. Option (c) divides the wrong way round.

questions.stem: A drawing pin is dropped 200 times and lands point-up 130 times. Using this experimental probability, how many times would you expect point-up in 500 drops?
questions.explanation: Experimental probability of point-up = 130/200 = 0.65. Expected in 500 drops = 500 × 0.65 = 325. Option (a) incorrectly doubles the original count.

questions.stem: A dice is suspected of being biased. In 300 rolls, the results are: 1 (48), 2 (52), 3 (50), 4 (49), 5 (51), 6 (50). Which is the best conclusion?

options.text: The dice is clearly biased towards 2
The dice is clearly biased towards 1
The results suggest the dice is approximately fair
300 rolls is not enough to make any conclusion

questions.explanation: For a fair dice, expected frequency for each outcome = 300/6 = 50. All observed frequencies are very close to 50 (range 48-52). This suggests the dice is approximately fair. Small variations are expected due to randomness.

questions.stem: In an experiment, the relative frequency of an event after n trials is shown: 10 trials: 0.4, 50 trials: 0.34, 200 trials: 0.31, 1000 trials: 0.295. What is the best estimate for the theoretical probability?
questions.explanation: As the number of trials increases, the relative frequency tends towards the theoretical probability. The value after 1000 trials (0.295) is the most reliable, suggesting the theoretical probability is approximately 0.3.

questions.stem: A biased coin has P(heads) = 0.7. Which of the following is true?

options.text: In 10 flips, you will get exactly 7 heads
In 100 flips, the relative frequency of heads will be exactly 0.7
As the number of flips increases, the relative frequency of heads tends to get closer to 0.7
After getting 3 tails in a row, heads is more likely on the next flip

questions.explanation: This is the law of large numbers: as trials increase, relative frequency approaches theoretical probability. Options (a) and (b) state exact results, which is incorrect since probability doesn't guarantee exact outcomes. Option (d) is the gambler's fallacy.
